On 3 October 2026, @jack shared on @X a notice from @Apple App Review, which stated that Bitchat had been removed from the India App Store pursuant to a blocking order issued by @GoI_MeitY under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”). The notice further showed that Apple understood the order to mean that Bitchat ‘includes content that is illegal in India’, and on this basis cited a violation of Guideline 5 of its App Review Guidelines.

At present, the application is also reported to be unavailable on the @GooglePlay, and its official website is inaccessible on several Internet Service Providers.

What is Bitchat, and why does it matter?

Bitchat is a decentralised, peer-to-peer messaging app that works over Bluetooth mesh, with no internet or cellular connection, and no central server. Furthermore, it requires no mandatory user registration, and keeps messages secured with end-to-end encryption. Beyond privacy, its value is resilience, as it helps people communicate through the internet shutdowns that the government imposes during citizen protests. Bitchat’s popularity in India surged during the repeated, unconstitutional internet shutdowns imposed by the government around Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, at the time of the NEET UG protests in July 2026.

Blocked through an Unconstitutional Procedure

According to Apple’s App Review notice, Bitchat has been blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 (“Blocking Rules 2009”). Jack Dorsey’s post on X suggests that the developers were neither heard nor served with a blocking order before the application was blocked. He learned of the block only through Apple’s notice, which is all he was able to share.

In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (paras 114 and 115), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the blocking procedure under Section 69A read with the Blocking Rules 2009, by heavily relying on the procedural safeguards built into this power, including, (1) recording of reasons in writing in the blocking order, which would be amenable to challenge in a writ petition, and (2) opportunity of hearing to the originator of the information before the order is passed under Rule 8. However, in consistent practice, the procedure under the Blocking Rules 2009 is applied in a manner that defeats these safeguards, rendering the blocking process under Section 69A and the Blocking Rules unconstitutional, as follows:

- By relying on the expression ‘person or intermediary’ in Rule 8, notice is invariably served only upon the intermediary and never upon the originator, even under normal circumstances. This practice egregiously deprives the originator of a fair opportunity to present their case against the request or complaint for blocking their information, thereby constituting a violation of the principles of natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem. This ultimately culminates in a situation where the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is curtailed without following a due and fair procedure in accordance with Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

- Furthermore, Rule 16 imposes an overarching requirement of confidentiality regarding requests and complaints for blocking information, as well as the actions taken thereon, including the final blocking order restricting public access to the information. This confidentiality provision enables the government agency to withhold, and simultaneously impedes the intermediary from providing, all relevant details to the affected person/originator of the information in a transparent manner.

- When combined with the practice followed under Rule 8, Rule 16 prevents the affected person from furnishing clarifications or a response to the blocking request, thereby depriving them of a fair opportunity to present their case. Furthermore, the affected person or originator is also deprived of a reasoned order blocking their information. This constitutes a clear violation of the principles of natural justice. Moreover, the above culminates in a situation where information is blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act, restricting the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression, through a procedure that is manifestly arbitrary and devoid of procedural fairness.

The blocking of Bitchat is not an isolated instance. Over time, India has witnessed an increasing trend of opaque information blocking under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules 2009, without any intimation to the affected person or originator, let alone furnishing them with the blocking order. These concerns were recently brought into sharp focus once again when @Cockroachisback's  X account was blocked without any transparency in May 2026.

Alarmed by this pattern and concerned about the violation of citizens’ digital and constitutional rights, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 filed a Public Interest Litigation in February 2025 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, challenging, inter alia, the legality of Rules 8 and 16 of the Blocking Rules 2009, as violative of Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India. The case is titled ‘Software Freedom Law Center, India and Anr. v. Union of India and Anr.’, bearing W.P.(C) No. 161/2025, and is presently pending for further adjudication before the Supreme Court.

In the said Petition, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has sought that Rule 16 ought to be struck down as unconstitutional, being violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, it has prayed that Rule 8 either be struck down as unconstitutional or be read down to interpret “or” as “and”, thereby mandatorily requiring the issuance of notice to the originator of information, ensuring conformity with the Constitution.

The illegal blocking of Bitchat

As of now, no blocking order is publicly available, and without it the specific grounds relied upon cannot be assailed. In any event, using Section 69A of the IT Act to block an entire application that enables communication is highly disproportionate.

Furthermore, the block immediately followed the internet shutdown imposed by the government on 2 October 2026 during a protest at Jantar Mantar. This timing gives rise to a strong inference that the application may have been targeted because it enables communication during internet shutdowns and protests. Enabling communication among protesters cannot, in any circumstance, be a valid ground for blocking an application under Article 19(2) or Section 69A.

Moreover, when the Delhi High Court upheld such exercise of power under Section 69A in ‘Telegram FZ LLC & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.’, 2026:DHC:5145, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 noted that the judgment set a dangerous precedent. Interpreting “information” in Section 69A so expansively as to permit the blocking of an entire application can have far-reaching adverse consequences, particularly by allowing communication channels to be disabled during protests.

Without prejudice to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s position that the decision sets a dangerous precedent, the Delhi High Court itself heavily relied on the temporary nature of the ban in reaching its conclusion. Here, the ban appears to be indefinite, which makes it all the more disproportionate and unconstitutional.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly urges the government to withdraw its orders directing Apple, Google and internet service providers to block the Bitchat application, as such orders are unconstitutional and violate citizens’ rights under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 also calls upon Apple to firmly stand by the fundamental rights of its users in India. Apple should not give effect to the order mechanically, and should diligently take all appropriate steps, including legal remedies, to ensure that it does not become complicit in the violation of its users' fundamental rights.

Bitchat, the messaging app made by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, has been removed from app stores in India.

Bitchat does not need the internet or a mobile network. Phones close to each other pass messages along over Bluetooth, so it keeps working even during an internet shutdown. Messages are encrypted and there is no central server.

The IT ministry ordered the removal on 3 October under Section 69A of the IT Act, the law the government uses to block websites and apps. The app is gone from Apple's App Store and Google Play in India, and its website does not open on many Indian internet providers.

In July, authorities had already asked GitHub to take down its code. The reason given then was that police cannot easily intercept or trace messages on it, and that it works during shutdowns.

India made up about 85% of all Bitchat downloads in one week of July, up from about 1% the month before.

The Internet Freedom Foundation, a digital rights group, says the law allows blocking unlawful content, not blocking an app because it works during shutdowns.

Meet Thomas, a 35-year-old who got hooked to FanDuel and DraftKings in the pandemic, ended up $50,000 in the red. He filed for bankruptcy and signed up for a Pennsylvania registry that banned him from using betting apps.

More recently, he saw an ad for Kalshi offering a cash bonus. He got the app and couldn’t put it down. He’s now living with his mom and grandmother and taking loans from them to afford food and car insurance payments. “I have a gambling addiction” he wrote to Kalshi, begging for them to ban him, which they eventually did. But not before he was more than $25,000 in the hole. 

Thomas represents dark side of the prediction market boom: Problem gamblers who relapse with Kalshi, which has blanketed TV, social media, sports stadiums, bus stations, trains, with ads trying to attract new traders, just as they insist they are not a gambling operator. That means they don’t honor “self-exclusion” registries maintained by states like Pennsylvania. Mental health clinicians say that creates a loophole for people like Thomas. 

What really got Thomas were Kalshi’s 15-minute crypto markets, where you can make a binary trade on whether Bitcoin will be above or below a certain number every 15 minutes. There were times he was betting 18 hours a day in these markets. 

He told me: “The odds flip so quickly. It’s such a rush. And when I’d lose, my brain just kept wanting to win it back. I never even traded Bitcoin or any crypto, but I just kept coming back to the rush of how unpredictable the markets were.”

An open letter to all my countrymen.

Do you want India to remain a democracy? Then you must understand what Gyanesh Kumar, the CEC, and his bosses are doing in the so-called SIR.
They are violating the law.
-  As per Section 21 of the law, a special revision is to be undertaken only in special cases, for reasons to be recorded in writing in each case; and that also only in any constituency or part of a constituency. An order for intensive revision for the whole country was illegal. An exception allowed for special cases cannot become the rule. The Supreme Court order upholding the general SIR was wrong.
Another question is - who took the decision for SIR in the whole country? Was it the full commission; or only Gyanesh Kumar.
-  Section 21 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, provides that where the revision of an electoral roll is taken up, the electoral roll in force at the time of the issue of the notification of revision shall continue in effect till the completion of the revision. The revised electoral rolls become complete only after all the appeals filed against inclusion or deletion are disposed off. Where the appeals were still pending, the original Electoral roll which was valid on the date of notification was to be used. Contrary to this the new roll with deletions was used during the elections even though appeals against deletions were still pending. This was illegal.

-  Section 22 of the RP Act provides that the Electoral Registration Officer, and not anyone else, can remove a voter's name from the roll and that also only on the grounds listed in Section 22(a), (b), and (c); and only after a specific enquiry, after giving the concerned person a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and only after appeals against his order are disposed off. Gyanesh Kumar removed the names of all the voters who had been listed by the ERO's after 2003, without any basis, without any enquiry, and without any show cause to the registered voters. This was blatantly illegal.
              The persons whose names were removed summarily had to apply as fresh voters in Form 6 and give evidence that they were eligible to be registered. This is a clear violation of the Supreme Court judgement in Lal Babu Hussain and Others v. Electoral Registration Officer and Others, [(1995) 3 SCC 100], which held that the enquiry authority or the objector and not the voter - must bring forth material evidence to back any claim that an enrolled voter be disqualified. And in such cases the voter must be asked to show cause why his name should not be removed on the basis of the grounds adduced by the enquiry officer. All this did not happen.

          The established jurisprudence is that the onus to prove that there are sufficient grounds for subjecting any person to a disability or punishment is on the
person or institution which is seeking to inflict the punishment. Here, Gyanesh Kumar has inverted the burden of proof. This is also against the law.

           Up to now, the efforts of the Government and the Election Commission have always been to enroll all eligible voters. It was a mission to deepen democracy and empower all citizens. This is the first time in history of the country that the mission is to disenfranchise people.

            Gyanesh Kumar added a new appendix to Form 6. He was not authorised to do so, as Form 6 is mandated by statutory rules. And he added this himself – against the views of the two election commissioners. The decisions of the commission are to be taken either unanimously – or by a majority. The majority was against the addition of the new appendix to the form. So the addition of the new appendix was against the decisions of the Commission itself. So why was it added? On whose orders? This was illegal. This appendix asks the applicant to state the serial number in the 2003 voter list on which their parents' names were listed. Where can an ordinary person – a young man of 18; access the 2003 roll in 2026? This stopped the registration of all young voters. BJP knows that young voters will not vote for it.

           Objections to inclusion of voters names in form 7 were filed in bulk. Who filed them? How were the forms accepted and acted upon when the persons who signed it did not appear?

           Names of 16 lac voters found valid by the ERO were not registered in Bengal because, it seems, the EC filed appeals against them. Why? On which grounds? Who authorised the Commission to file appeals? Two Election Commissioners say they did not do so. So the Commission did not authorise anyone to file appeals. Who did it? Gyanesh Kumar? These people were prevented from voting in the election.
 
             So the Election Commission and some people from a political party were acting in cahoots  to get bogus Form 7 objections filed in bulk and delete names?
 
             How were elections allowed to be held when the appeals of lakhs of voters were pending? The ECI and the Supreme Court have to answer. The appeals which have been decided show that 90% of the voters who were left out were valid.

            A ridiculous thing was brought up called "logical discrepancy". Gyanesh Kumar does not have any idea of how the poor live in India. Their children are not born in hospitals. They do not have birth certificates. They do not have calendars in their homes. When the BLO approached them to enroll them in the voter list they gave their estimated year of birth. Similarly, when their fathers' names were enrolled in the electoral roll, they gave their estimated year of birth. The dumb people in the Election Commission, under Gyanesh Kumar, said that any difference of less than 15 years between father and children would be a logical discrepancy justifying excluding their names. The “Logical Discrepancy” names were excluded without enquiry, contrary to sec 21 of the act.

             The largest number of exclusions have been the poor and the underprivileged, those without a voice. They were and are mostly away from their homes, earning their daily bread. Lakhs are working in faraway places/states. They could not and cannot afford to go back to their homes for a month to get their names registered. They will go hungry if they do not earn. They cannot fill the complicated forms. They do not have birth certificates and the papers. Why should they sacrifice their daily wages for a vote?

             The illegal immigrants are not affected. The first thing they do on entering India is to get their documentation made—Aadhaar card, ration card, etc. The earlier immigrants are their support systems. It is the poor Indian citizens who have been disenfranchised. The dumb people in the Election Commission and their bosses did not understand this. Or they wanted it this way.

              Gyanesh Kumar has made a digital electoral roll and empowered it to refuse addition of names because of “Logical discrepancy”. In the name of "Logical discrepancy", the names of millions of voters have not been included. This is against the law. The only authority designated by law to add or delete names and publish the electoral rolls is the Electoral Registration Officer. Contrary to this, the electoral roll was centralised and the revision happened centrally. This was illegal.

            Two Election Commissioners pointed out that the only people authorized to add or delete names – the ERO, the DEO and the CEO were not being allowed to access the voter list. In Goa, 97 electors were found by the ERO to be valid and fit for inclusion in the roll. They have not been able to add their names to the roll as yet.

             The centralisation of the voter list amendment is dangerous. It can be used to cut voters from booths which vote against NDA. Is this what happened?

            Deleting voters names before verification is a heinous offence, and Gyanesh Kumar is guilty thereof.

            13 crores names have been deleted by SIR so far. This is 13% of the voters, and SIR is not over. The difference between NDA and INDIA in the 2024 elections was only 3%. So the deletion have had and will have a material impact on the elections.

text:
Statement on restrictions faced by cartoonists Satish Acharya and Manjul on Instagram

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restrictions faced by cartoonists @satishacharya and @MANJULtoons on Instagram. On 26th September, Manjul’s cartoon on the Election Commission was restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement.” 

Satish Acharya also repeatedly faced takedowns of his posts on Instagram, and on 28th September, his account got restricted in India. The notification shared by the cartoonist stated that the platform had to “repeatedly restrict access to content posted” by him “pursuant to legal requirements.”

In March 2026, Satish also received two notifications from @X stating that @GoI_MeitY had ordered the platform to block his content. He also received a notification from X about a content takedown request from the Cyber Crime Department of the Mumbai Police. These cartoons depicted India’s stance on US-Israel bombing on Iran and the killing of its supreme leader. Another cartoon showed the arms of state actors forming a human chain around billionaire Gautam Adani with the caption “Ek hain to safe hain.”

These notifications also stated that the platform could not provide him with additional information due to legal restrictions. This lack of transparency makes it particularly difficult to challenge a blocking order. While notifications issued by X identified the authorities that ordered the takedowns, Instagram did not disclose which authorities had ordered the takedowns. In such instances, before a creator can even consider approaching a court, they may first have to determine which government authority issued the order, under what legal provision it was issued, and what specific content or reasoning formed the basis for it. Without access to this information, exercising the right to challenge the restriction becomes significantly harder. 

Even when the information is available, going to court requires time, money, and legal assistance. All of these resources may not even be available for cartoonists, independent creators, or students. For someone facing multiple takedown orders, challenging each restriction individually can become an exhausting and expensive exercise.

@scroll_in’s article on the restrictions faced by Satish Acharya stated that the cartoonist attempted to challenge Meta’s action but was unable to reach Instagram’s help centre due to its automated grievance redressal systems and the lack of access to human support. Meta’s AI Support Assistant provides ‘In-App Appeal’ as the ‘primary method for challenging a content decision.’ However, this method is not a statutory remedy, amenable to further challenge at the Grievance Appellate Committee level. The prescribed procedure of approaching the Grievance Officer through Meta’s official reporting form does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or takedowns through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.”

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also observed that the Grievance Officer email address available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Officer report. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies, such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

In the past few months, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has recorded similar instances of restrictions faced by other cartoonists in India. In August 2026, @cartoonistrrs's posts showing a comical representation of the PM’s viral reel received a takedown notice, and @cartoonistvish faced 4 takedown orders for his cartoon criticising Prime Minister Narender Modi’s foreign travels during domestic issues. Even a simple satire by @BagchiAsh, showing the PM with a Melody chocolate on his forehead, was restricted on Meta.

Over time, such instances of censorship can have consequences far beyond individual takedowns. When creators repeatedly see their work removed without clear explanations and realise that the only meaningful way to challenge the decision may be through costly legal proceedings, they may begin to censor themselves. The uncertainty surrounding what can be taken down and the difficulty of fighting back when takedowns happen can eventually discourage people from creating altogether. If the cost of speaking becomes too high and the consequences too unpredictable, creators may censor themselves or give up on their art entirely.

The increasing trend of censorship of cartoons and political humour is deeply concerning, particularly because it points to a shrinking space for dissent in India. The right to freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right, and the ability to question, criticise and even ridicule those in power is an essential part of a democratic society. Dissent may be uncomfortable for governments, but discomfort cannot be the basis for silencing it.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon @Meta to remove restrictions on Satish Acharya’s posts and account and Manjul’s Instagram posts with immediate effect. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions on cartoons and satirical content. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues for content takedowns and account restrictions.

text:
The Federal Government has closed down more than 13 million social media accounts due to offensive content.

The federal government has shut down approximately 13,597,057 social media accounts due to offensive content and breaches of the code of conduct by users on platforms like TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, and X (previously known as Twitter).

The government action was detailed in a 2024 Compliance Report on the Code of Practice, which was provided to the government by companies operating interactive computer service platforms, including Google, Microsoft, and TikTok, among others.

The Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), and the National Broadcasting Commission (NBC) collaboratively released the Code of Practice.

In an announcement made on Wednesday, Hajiya Hadiza Umar, the Director of Corporate Communications and Media Relations at NITDA, stated that the government had removed a total of 58,909,112 offensive pieces of content from various platforms.

The statement reads in part: “The compliance reports provide valuable insights into the platforms’ efforts to address user safety concerns in line with the Code of Practice and the platforms’ community guidelines.

“The submission of these reports marks a significant step towards fostering a safer and responsible digital environment for Nigerian users.

“It also demonstrates the platforms’ commitment to ensuring a secure and trustworthy online environment for all.

“This achievement reflects the provisions of the Code of Practice, which mandates that large service platforms are registered in Nigeria and comply with relevant laws, including the fulfilment of their tax obligation, while reinforcing the commitment to online safety for Nigerians.

“While NITDA acknowledges these commendable efforts, we emphasise that building a safer digital space requires sustained collaboration and engagement among all stakeholders.

“We remain committed to working with industry players, civil society, and regulatory partners to further strengthen user safety measures, enhance digital literacy, and promote trust and transparency in Nigeria’s digital ecosystem.”

text:
“Maybe Maa Sita Blessed Her To Take This Action”
Kudos And Congratulations Amita Ji

In a significant legal update, tech giant Google has informed the Delhi High Court that a controversial video uploaded by popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been officially withheld from viewers across India. The dispute centers around a video titled “Can Hindus Eat BEEF? | Kerala Story 2 EXPOSED”, which Rathee uploaded in March.

Advocate @SachdevaAmita (Amita Sachdeva) filed a petition alleging that the video contained “false, misleading, and provocative statements” claiming that Hindu deities Lord Ram, Lord Krishna, and Goddess Sita consumed meat and alcohol. She argued this severely hurt the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus.

Following a High Court order to expedite the grievance on July 3, the Central Government's Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) directed Google on July 15 to remove the video within 24 hours.

The petitioner has pushed for a global injunction, pointing out that the video remains accessible globally and via Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) inside India, viewing geo-blocking as “partial compliance”.

Presiding Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma noted that Google has executed what it can under current domestic boundaries, as the broader legal issue regarding global takedown mandates is already pending before a separate Division Bench of the High Court.

Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, representing the government, argued that offensive videos should be blocked across the board to avoid a repetitive game of legal cat-and-mouse with duplicates. The court has adjourned the matter for its next hearing on September 3.

India's platforms are legally required to notify users when their content gets taken down by government order — but compliance is spotty at best.
The rule exists under the Information Technology Act's intermediary framework. When a platform receives a government takedown notice, users are supposed to get an explanation: what was removed, why, and which authority issued it.
In practice, most platforms either ignore this entirely or send vague notices after the fact. No timeline is enforced. No standardized format exists. Users often discover their content is gone only when they try to access it.
Former MeitY (Ministry of Electronics and IT) cyber-law officials have flagged this gap repeatedly. The logic was simple: transparency about state censorship creates a paper trail, deters overreach, and lets users contest removals.
But India's digital ecosystem treats the notification rule as optional. WhatsApp doesn't notify for group bans. Twitter (now X) batches notices weeks later. YouTube compliance varies by region. TikTok, before its ban, rarely proactively informed users.
The enforcement gap matters because:
• There is no penalty structure — platforms face no fines or license consequences for skipping notification.
• Users have no realistic way to challenge removals without knowing they happened or why.
• Government agencies know the lack of oversight means takedowns go undocumented.
• A parallel system of private censorship operates without the judicial review that formal bans would trigger.
The fix would require either stricter intermediary rules with real penalties, or a centralized notification registry — both politically difficult in India's current regulatory environment.
As government content moderation requests accelerate globally, India's notification gap is becoming a template for how to make state censorship functionally invisible.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

TMC Splits
SC Senior Advocate Mahesh Jethmalani Decodes The Legal Reality Of Faction Mergers

Senior Supreme Court advocate Mahesh Jethmalani clarified that the rebel Trinamool Congress (TMC) MPs who moved to merge with the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI) are legally protected under the anti-defection law, provided they meet the two-thirds threshold. He explained that a merger backed by two-thirds of the legislature party provides a "safe harbour" from parliamentary disqualification under Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule of the Indian Constitution.

Under Paragraph 4 of the Tenth Schedule, a breakaway faction is legally immune to disqualification if at least two-thirds of the members of the Legislature Party agree to merge with another political entity. With 20 rebel MPs splitting from TMC's 29-member lower house strength, they satisfy this legal benchmark.

Jethmalani explicitly ruled out any "dual membership" or subsequent claims to the original party. Once a faction chooses to merge with a new or existing entity like the NCPI, they entirely forfeit their right to claim the original TMC identity, name, or party symbol.

He noted a critical distinction between the current TMC crisis and the 2022 Shiv Sena split. In the Shiv Sena and NCP (Ajit Pawar) episodes, rival factions battled internally to claim they were the "real" original party. In contrast, the TMC rebels are actively executing a legal merger into a completely different registered political party, meaning they cannot double-back to claim the TMC brand.

Jethmalani dismissed political criticisms regarding the choice of the merging entity, stating there is nothing unconstitutional about merging with any registered political party, regardless of its size, optics, or lack of significant electoral footprint.

He observed that the current anti-defection framework inadvertently facilitates mass group defections via mergers while restricting individual floor-crossing, ultimately shifting political battles into lengthy judicial overhauls.

Statement on restrictions faced by cartoonists Satish Acharya and Manjul on Instagram

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restrictions faced by cartoonists @satishacharya and @MANJULtoons on Instagram. On 26th September, Manjul’s cartoon on the Election Commission was restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement.” 

Satish Acharya also repeatedly faced takedowns of his posts on Instagram, and on 28th September, his account got restricted in India. The notification shared by the cartoonist stated that the platform had to “repeatedly restrict access to content posted” by him “pursuant to legal requirements.”

In March 2026, Satish also received two notifications from @X stating that @GoI_MeitY had ordered the platform to block his content. He also received a notification from X about a content takedown request from the Cyber Crime Department of the Mumbai Police. These cartoons depicted India’s stance on US-Israel bombing on Iran and the killing of its supreme leader. Another cartoon showed the arms of state actors forming a human chain around billionaire Gautam Adani with the caption “Ek hain to safe hain.”

These notifications also stated that the platform could not provide him with additional information due to legal restrictions. This lack of transparency makes it particularly difficult to challenge a blocking order. While notifications issued by X identified the authorities that ordered the takedowns, Instagram did not disclose which authorities had ordered the takedowns. In such instances, before a creator can even consider approaching a court, they may first have to determine which government authority issued the order, under what legal provision it was issued, and what specific content or reasoning formed the basis for it. Without access to this information, exercising the right to challenge the restriction becomes significantly harder. 

Even when the information is available, going to court requires time, money, and legal assistance. All of these resources may not even be available for cartoonists, independent creators, or students. For someone facing multiple takedown orders, challenging each restriction individually can become an exhausting and expensive exercise.

@scroll_in’s article on the restrictions faced by Satish Acharya stated that the cartoonist attempted to challenge Meta’s action but was unable to reach Instagram’s help centre due to its automated grievance redressal systems and the lack of access to human support. Meta’s AI Support Assistant provides ‘In-App Appeal’ as the ‘primary method for challenging a content decision.’ However, this method is not a statutory remedy, amenable to further challenge at the Grievance Appellate Committee level. The prescribed procedure of approaching the Grievance Officer through Meta’s official reporting form does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or takedowns through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.”

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also observed that the Grievance Officer email address available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Officer report. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies, such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

In the past few months, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has recorded similar instances of restrictions faced by other cartoonists in India. In August 2026, @cartoonistrrs's posts showing a comical representation of the PM’s viral reel received a takedown notice, and @cartoonistvish faced 4 takedown orders for his cartoon criticising Prime Minister Narender Modi’s foreign travels during domestic issues. Even a simple satire by @BagchiAsh, showing the PM with a Melody chocolate on his forehead, was restricted on Meta.

Over time, such instances of censorship can have consequences far beyond individual takedowns. When creators repeatedly see their work removed without clear explanations and realise that the only meaningful way to challenge the decision may be through costly legal proceedings, they may begin to censor themselves. The uncertainty surrounding what can be taken down and the difficulty of fighting back when takedowns happen can eventually discourage people from creating altogether. If the cost of speaking becomes too high and the consequences too unpredictable, creators may censor themselves or give up on their art entirely.

The increasing trend of censorship of cartoons and political humour is deeply concerning, particularly because it points to a shrinking space for dissent in India. The right to freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right, and the ability to question, criticise and even ridicule those in power is an essential part of a democratic society. Dissent may be uncomfortable for governments, but discomfort cannot be the basis for silencing it.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon @Meta to remove restrictions on Satish Acharya’s posts and account and Manjul’s Instagram posts with immediate effect. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions on cartoons and satirical content. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues for content takedowns and account restrictions.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

On September 29, 2026, Trump signed Executive Order 14433, “Eliminating Disease-Carrying Pests and Restoring Enjoyment of the Great Outdoors.” It is aimed at cutting invasive mosquitoes in Washington, D.C. by about 90 percent and ticks by about 50 percent by 2028, mainly on federal land, using habitat cleanup, non-chemical methods, and newer tools.
The order tells the EPA, with Agriculture and HHS, to submit a regulatory framework within about 60 days for advanced tick and mosquito control. That framework is supposed to consider sterilization techniques, “safe genetic modification,” and beneficial bacteria, and to speed registration of methods the EPA finds safe and effective. It does not itself authorize the release of genetically modified mosquitoes or ticks.
What the post gets wrong:
•  It does not “legalize gene mosquitoes and gene ticks” this week. It orders a review framework. As of a May 27, 2026 EPA fact check, no genetically engineered mosquito releases were authorized in the U.S.; an earlier experimental-use permit had expired in 2024.
•  Bill Gates is not named in the order or the White House fact sheet. The Gates Foundation has funded mosquito-control work for years (including Oxitec-style modified mosquitoes and related disease research), but this order is not a Gates product rollout, and there is no public statement from him about it.
•  “Gene ticks” are not a current commercial program the order greenlights. Sterile-insect and bacteria-based (for example Wolbachia) mosquito releases already exist as separate techniques; genetic modification is only one option the framework must consider.
So the executive order is real and does open the door to biotech pest control, including possible genetic methods if regulators later approve them. The claim that Trump just cleared Bill Gates’ gene mosquitoes and gene ticks is not what the order says.

THE VIBE MANUFACTURING PLAYBOOK

1. Measure everything. Digital calipers for small parts, a phone LiDAR app like Polycam to scan a space or an object. Bad measurements are the #1 reason first builds fail

2. Have a frontier model write the design as code. Describe the part to a model like Claude Opus 5.5 or Astra, and have it write the design in a codebased CAD tool like OpenSCAD or CadQuery. Zoo's Text to CAD does it in one step!

3. Use real CAD files. The text to 3D models on Hugging Face make shapes that look right, but factories need precise files: STEP for machined parts, DXF for lasercut metal, STL for 3D printing

4. Make sure it can be made. Ask the AI to check the design against how factories actually work: how tight metal can bend, how small a hole can be, how much wiggle room parts need etc...

5. Prototype in plastic first. A $300 to $600 home 3D printer like a Bambu Lab lets you test the fit overnight before paying for metal (really fun to play with too!)

6. Pay an engineer for 1 hour. Before your first real order, have a mechanical engineer on Upwork etc review the files. It's the cheapest insurance you'll ever buy.

7. Send it out. SendCutSend cuts and bends metal, Xometry and Protolabs handle machining and plastic, JLCPCB builds circuit boards. Instant quotes, and parts usually ship in days.

8. Add the brains. Most smart features run on a cheap wifi chip like the ESP32. Design the board in KiCad, and use ESPHome to control it straight from your phone.

9. Make one, then fix it. Your first version will be off somewhere! Order a single unit, test it, and adjust.

10. Do the math. Add up parts, finishing, assembly, packaging, and shipping. Custom products are hard to resell, so price for healthy margins.

11. Sell the design and make to order. Let customers adjust the measurements, and only manufacture after they pay. Zero warehouse, zero unsold stock.

12. Handle the boring part. If it plugs into a wall or touches kids, you'll need safety certification. It's slow and annoying, which is exactly why it's a moat.

13. Scale when it works. Once orders are steady, switch to batch runs and your cost per unit drops fast.

text:
$ASTS - Elon Musk has lost the space mobile race before it even began.

Source: CE Noticias Financieras (Latin America)

The fiercest space race isn't about returning to the moon. It's about allowing you to make a TikTok or watch Netflix on your phone anywhere on the planet, from the salt flats of Atacama to the dunes of Khongor in the Gobi Desert. To make this happen, two radically different design philosophies are at war, and several companies are building the infrastructure needed to ensure that every phone on the planet is permanently connected to the Internet.

On one side is Elon Musk's SpaceX--and all the imitators that have followed in Starlink's wake. Their approach is to invade space with tens of thousands of satellites, creating a network of objects covering low Earth orbit. On the other side is a small Texas-based company called AST SpaceMobile, which believes it can provide better service with fewer than 100 satellites in space.

Both companies--along with Amazon and a handful of Chinese organizations--want to dominate global wireless communications. The satellite constellation with the fastest service, the widest coverage, the best compatibility with 5G mobile phones, and the lowest operating costs will dominate how we communicate in the coming years. The prevailing approach will have a serious impact not only on the future of the internet, but also on the health of our planet and the future of the internet and humanity in space.

A new era of space race

SpaceX, owner of Starlink, launched the first satellite in 2019, providing broadband Internet access to anyone with a large Starlink antenna and a modem on the ground. Since then, it has put more than 9,000 satellites into orbit. The company plans to have a constellation of 34,000 satellites. Following Starlink's initial launch, several competitors followed suit, including Jeff Bezos and his Kuiper constellation--now called Amazon Leo--and the Chinese, whose plans include up to 250,000 satellites.

But there is a fundamental problem with this megaconstellation design: Musk's plan for space internet is a flawed , wasteful, and dangerous game of orbital Russian roulette .

Scientists are concerned that Starlink's projected constellation of 34,400 satellites (which could reach up to 75,000) will cause irreparable damage to the atmosphere. A large-scale constellation also dramatically increases the possibility of a space collision that could start a catastrophic chain reaction, destroying orbital networks that are crucial to our survival as a species.

Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist and spaceflight historian at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, has been documenting satellite launches in his Jonathan's Space Report newsletter. He believes there may be better ways to achieve global satellite coverage, if we need to do so. "Personally, I prefer a smaller number of larger satellites," he tells me in a telephone interview. "One reason is the risk of space collisions. If you have 10 times more satellites, you have 100 times more near misses. So, just from that point of view, consolidating into a smaller number of satellites seems more sensible."

The better and more efficient alternative

That's where Musk's biggest competitor comes in. AST SpaceMobile has developed direct-to-mobile technology that uses large satellites called BlueBirds. These machines use thousands of antennas to deliver broadband coverage directly to standard mobile phones, says company president Scott Wisniewski.

"This approach is remarkably efficient: we can achieve global coverage with approximately 90 satellites, not thousands or even tens of thousands as other systems require," Wisniewski tells me in an email. McDowell agrees that AST's approach--if it succeeds in meeting its goals--is the best, most efficient, and least wasteful path forward.

The key is the size and sophistication of its satellites. AST's first generation of commercial satellites, BlueBird 1-5, are deployed in a huge 64.4-square-meter array in space. Today, the company has five BlueBird 1-5 satellites operating in orbit, but its ambitions are much greater. On December 24, AST launched the first of its new-generation satellites from India--called Block 2--and it broke records. BlueBird 6 has a surface area of nearly 223 square meters, making it the largest single satellite in low Earth orbit. The company plans to launch up to 60 more by the end of 2026.

"This large surface area is essential for capturing weak signals from standard, unmodified mobile phones on the ground," explains Wisniewski. "It is, in essence, a single, extremely powerful and sensitive cell tower in the sky, capable of serving a huge geographic area... This design philosophy directly addresses the two biggest threats posed by the megaconstellation model." First, with only about 90 Block 2 satellites needed for global coverage, the absolute volume of material launched and removed from orbit is orders of magnitude less than the tens of thousands planned by SpaceX and others. With a lifespan of 7 to 10 years, AST satellites are designed to outlast Starlink satellites, which have a lifespan of about 5 years. This combination of factors dramatically reduces the potential for atmospheric pollution.

In addition, fewer satellites dramatically reduce the risk of orbital collisions. "Fewer satellites in orbit inherently reduces the likelihood of collisions and the creation of space debris, promoting a more sustainable orbital environment," says Wisniewski. It is a solution based on precision engineering rather than brute numerical force, a testament to a different way of thinking about the problem.

As McDowell says, from a space traffic perspective, "fewer and larger satellites is probably better." It is a design choice that prioritizes sustainability and risk mitigation. And the total cost, much lower in the case of AST.

A reckless brute force plan

The central idea behind Starlink's direct-to-mobile service is brute force. It's the digital equivalent of saturation bombing: saturating low Earth orbit with tens of thousands of relatively small, cheap, and disposable satellites. Each one acts like a small cell tower in the sky, talking to the phone in your pocket. Because they are in low orbit, latency is minimal and the signal is strong enough for a standard phone. It's a simple concept, but its elegance is deceptive. In reality, it has the elegance of a greasy sandwich.

The Starlink model is based on a constant cycle of replacement. After about five years, they are programmed to fall back to Earth, disintegrating upon reentry. This is where the first major problem arises .

"When they disintegrate, they don't just vanish," McDowell explains. "They turn into dust, alumina dust, aluminum oxide particles. These particles are very effective at destroying ozone."

The long-term effect of depositing tons of this material into the upper atmosphere every day is a terrifying unknown. We are, in effect, conducting an uncontrolled experiment on our own planet's protective layers. McDowell points out that while a single rocket launch causes temporary, localized damage to the ozone, the continuous reentry of thousands of satellites creates a persistent, global problem that has never been studied on this scale.

SpaceX aggressively dismissed these concerns in 2021 in a legal battle with Viasat, a rival satellite internet service for home, business, and military use. Its legal defense directly attacked the scientific premise that satellites create harmful amounts of aluminum oxide when they burn up. The company has been ignoring warnings about potential ozone depletion since 2024.

Musk has attempted to address light pollution. Faced with protests from the astronomical community over the brightness of its satellites, they iterated on their design. First came DarkSat, an experimental coating that proved ineffective. Then came VisorSat, a deployable sunshade that blocked light reflection on the brightest parts of the satellite.

Now, McDowell tells me, they are using a dielectric mirror film that reflects less light back to Earth. "They have made a significant effort to reduce brightness, and the newer Starlink satellites are substantially dimmer than the early ones," he admits. "But they are still bright enough to be a problem for large tracking telescopes like the Vera Rubin Observatory."

These mitigation efforts, while commendable, only address a relatively minor problem--light pollution--and do nothing to solve the more fundamental problems of atmospheric pollution and orbital saturation. The problem is compounded by the fact that everyone is now copying this model. Amazon's Project Leo plans to launch more than 3,200 satellites... Beijing and some Chinese companies were planning two separate megaconstellations, Guowang and G60 Starlink, with a total of nearly 26,000 satellites. "We are only at the beginning of this, " warns McDowell. "And that becomes very worrying because now it's not just one company, it's a lot of companies." To further increase his concerns, just a few days ago the Chinese government requested launch permits for 200,000 satellites.

AST's approach is not without its own controversies. The size of its satellites makes them very bright in the night sky, a major source of frustration for astronomers on the ground. McDowell confirms that when it was launched in 2022, AST's prototype satellite, BlueWalker 3, became "one of the ten brightest objects in the night sky for a while."

"It's a serious problem, and we're working directly with the astronomical community to mitigate our impact," Wisniewski tells me. The company is exploring solutions such as anti-reflective coatings and operational adjustments to minimize the time its satellites are at their brightest. However, McDowell is not aware of anyone working with AST SpaceMobile, and the latter did not provide any details.

According to McDowell, however, the size and brightness is a reasonable trade-off. "Even though the BlueBirds are bright, there aren't that many of them. So I kind of prefer that approach," he says. "As long as they don't change their criteria and say, 'Actually, we need 30,000 of these too.'" But we know that AST's design and technology doesn't need those numbers. Musk does.

An orbital game of Russian roulette

Beyond environmental concerns, there is an even more immediate existential threat: Kessler syndrome. Popularized by the movie Gravity, it is a scenario that keeps space experts like McDowell awake at night. The theory, proposed by NASA scientist Donald Kessler in 1978, describes a domino effect in which a collision between two objects in orbit creates a cloud of debris. Each piece of that debris then becomes a projectile that can cause another collision, creating even more debris, until low Earth orbit becomes an impassable minefield of hypervelocity shrapnel.

"The more satellites you have, the greater the probability of a collision," McDowell states plainly. "And the problem is that once you have the first collision, the debris from it now threatens all the other satellites."

SpaceX has designed a highly automated collision avoidance system for Starlink, and McDowell acknowledges its sophistication. Its satellites constantly monitor their trajectories and can autonomously fire their thrusters to avoid potential impacts. "They perform thousands of maneuvers per month," he says, which is a testament both to the capability of the system and the terribly crowded environment in which it operates. In total, they have performed 50,000 evasive maneuvers since 2019.

But while SpaceX claims its satellites are 100% safe, the facts tell us they are not infallible. "Even with a 99% success rate in deorbiting, a one percent failure rate in a constellation of 30,000 satellites means you're adding 300 dead satellites weighing several hundred kilograms to orbit every five years," McDowell calculates. That's 300 uncontrollable bullets waiting to start the Kessler syndrome.

A catastrophic chain reaction could, in a matter of hours or days, wipe out the essential satellite networks that underpin modern civilization. This isn't just about losing your GPS navigation on the way to a new restaurant. It's about the collapse of global finance, weather forecasting, communications, and critical military and disaster response systems. We are talking about decades of technological regression, a scenario that McDowell finds increasingly plausible as more megaconstellations are launched. It is a high-stakes gamble with the essential infrastructure of civilization.

There is also a danger of direct impact to people on the ground. Some Starlink satellites have already failed in orbit, becoming uncontrollable space debris that fell back to Earth. There is at least one report of a piece of satellite hitting a building in Canada. The latest incident occurred on December 17, 2025, when a Starlink satellite experienced an anomaly, losing communication and causing a propellant tank purge, rapid orbital decay, and the release of debris into low Earth orbit. In a 2023 report to Congress, the FAA warns that there is a real risk that falling Starlink debris could injure or kill someone by 2035.

Space debris is also a problem for rockets. In early November, three taikonauts returned after being stranded at the Chinese international station for nine days. They were unable to use the spacecraft that was to take them back to Earth--the Chengdou-20--because orbital debris had previously struck it. The China Manned Space Agency said the astronauts found "tiny cracks" in a small window on their Shenzhou-20 spacecraft.

The impact was not fatal, but things could have gone very wrong. The Chinese, however, are not acting any differently. Beijing will launch hundreds of thousands of satellites that mimic Starlink's design. They are contributing to the problem and increasing the risk tothemselves and everyone else.

Why AST SpaceMobile can beat Musk

Right now, Starlink does not offer direct broadband to mobile phones; instead, it offers only limited text and data connections. This low-speed connectivity requires a line of sight to the satellite, as SpaceX states on its website. Starlink, despite its leading position in the satellite internet business market, is still trying to catch up on the direct-to-mobile front, and it is very likely that it will never be able to close the gap with AST. Certainly not in the short term, as Musk himself admits.

Musk's company has two huge factors working against it. First is the hardware in orbit. To provide broadband to phones, it needs a next-generation Starlink V3 satellite, which does not yet exist. And even if it did, SpaceX has no way to launch it. With an estimated weight of about 2,000 kilograms, the V3 satellite is too large and heavy for the Falcon 9 workhorse rocket to deploy in economically viable quantities. The entire business model for Starlink V3 dependson the success of Starship, Musk's next-generation super-heavy launchvehicle . But Starship is still in development and has not yet achieved the operational and consistent launch cadence necessary to deploy and maintain a constellation of thousands of V3 satellites.

But even if Musk manages to finish Starship and the Starlink V3 satellites on time, there is a second, even bigger hardware problem: broadband connectivity will not work unless the mobile phone has a special modem chip. Yes, space cadets, you will have to buy a new phone to enjoy Starlink connectivity, while AST works with any current unmodified phone. None of these new Starlink-enabled phones exist or have been announced yet. According to Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's chief operating officer, the company is now working on this chip.

"We are working with chip manufacturers to get the right chips in phones," she told the audience at Space Business Week in Paris last September. Expecting phone manufacturers to incorporate Starlink's proprietary modem into their phones seems like a lot to ask. Especially when manufacturers like Apple have their own plans for mobile-to-space connectivity. It seems unlikely that Tim Cook would tie the company's crown jewel to Musk's whims. Or make phones even more expensive... However,That doesn't even matter because even if Musk had 18,000 of these V3 satellites and Starships ready to launch, the problem would remain the same: you'll need phones with Starlink modems inside them for broadband. And the line-of-sight problem will persist. Broadband only works when the phone can "see" the satellites in the sky.

This is why Musk's initial timeline for direct-to-mobile broadband is entirely speculative. In fact, while Musk said it would be ready in 2026, SpaceX itself admitted that testing of the first phones equipped with Starlink chips is scheduled for 2026, and Starlink aims to complete its constellation of direct-to-mobile V3 satellites in 2027. It is a promise built on a promise, a technological if that depends on a logistical when. Meanwhile, AST SpaceMobile is preparing to launch new operational satellites on existing rockets. Now, Elon Musk himself has admitted that it will take at least two years to get the version 3 satellites into orbit and the phones with that chip. And as experience has shown us time and time again at Tesla, Neuralink, and SpaceX itself, when Musk says two years, it usually translates to six.

AST SpaceMobile has already proven that its technology works, with six operational satellites now transmitting at typical 5G speeds directly to regular phones. This does not mean it has a guaranteed victory against Starlink or any of its competitors. Although it has the capital to execute its plan--backed by investors such as AT&T, Alphabet, Rakuten, Vanguard, BlackRock, and Mexican magnate Carlos Slim, owner of Latin America's largest telecommunications operator--and superior technology, it needs to execute dozens of launches.

This confidence in the technology explains why the stock has soared 333% in a year, but doubts about potential execution problems also explain why the stock experiences wild swings. With every news of a launch or a launch delay, the stock can swing 10% or 20% up or down. That's why the market treats AST as a high-risk, high-reward battleground. It could be a billion-dollar business or explode on the launch pad if the company doesn't get all those satellites up by 2026.

The coup de grâce

This technological and philosophical divergence has not gone unnoticed by Musk. Seeing a direct threat to his ambitions, he has embarked on a campaign to undermine AST SpaceMobile, with baseless accusations, claiming that they are a danger in low Earth orbit due to the size of their satellites. At the same time, Musk is fighting his own problems in low Earth orbit. China has already reported two near-misses with Starlink satellites that caused its Tiangong space station to perform emergency evasive maneuvers. On January 2, SpaceX was forced to move 4,000 satellites into a lower orbit after new research by Chinese scientists highlighted the company's recklessness and the very real risk of collision.

In addition, Musk desperately tried to prevent the FCC from granting AST access to the necessary spectrum--the range of radio frequencies it needs for its satellites to connect to mobile phones on Earth--arguing that it would be "catastrophic" for its service because the powerful signals from AST's large satellites could interfere with Starlink user terminals. In response, AST SpaceMobile claims that its system is designed to coexist with other networks and operates entirely within internationally agreed limits established to prevent such interference. The FCC agreed and allowed AST to use the spectrum. And that move, if every logistical aspect is executed according to plan, gives AST a resounding victory over Musk.

Imagine the radio spectrum as a giant highway in the sky with a limited number of lanes. Carrying data back and forth, AST's trucks have the right to travel on a huge number of these lanes thanks to partners such as AT&T and Verizon. Approximately 35 MHz of what the industry calls the "golden low-band spectrum." It also acquired an extra 45 MHz of low-band spectrum from a bankrupt communications company called Ligado. That's a whopping 80 MHz. And remember the company's proprietary magic formula we mentioned earlier? That's AST's secret weapon for making this highway work, a chip that ties these different radio bands together into a single massive pipe, capable of delivering peak speeds of 120 Mbps to phones, comparable to your typical 5G connection.

SpaceX and its partner T-Mobile have very few lanes available right now: only 5 MHz. That's like comparing an 80-lane superhighway to a 5-lane street. To try to fix that, Musk has spent $17 billion to acquire 50 more lanes: 50 MHz of S-band spectrum from another bankrupt communications company, EchoStar. The problem lies in that "S," which stands for short. Physics dictates that lower frequency radio waves penetrate solid objects more effectively than higher frequency waves. Because L-band waves are longer (lower frequency), they are better at passing through non-metallic obstacles such as walls, foliage, and weather compared to the higher frequency S-band.

That's why Starlink's space-to-mobile service will require line of sight to work. Meanwhile, AST claims that its system will work indoors and outdoors, penetrating buildings in a similar way to a normal mobile signal. Wisniewski claims that a phone will connect through "a wall" and work through the roof of your car due to two factors: they use a low-frequency radio connection, and their satellites are large enough to "hear" and "talk" to phones on the ground even behind obstacles. However, this scenario has not yet been tested by the company or a third party. Only line-of-sight broadband with normal phones has been successfully tested multiple times. If it works inside cars and buildings as he claims, however, the user experience will be seamless. Your phone will simply have service where it didn't before, which will be provided through your existing carrier such as AT&T or Vodafone when it becomes operational sometime in 2026.

Should we really do this?

Scientific evidence and experts tell us that AST has everything it needs to win the next billion-dollar business race. If they execute their plan as they intend, Musk will have a very difficult time competing in space mobile telephony (unlike in home internet connectivity, with his Starlink satellite antennas).

But, whoever wins, should this race even exist? What if we are planning this competition for the wrong reasons?

Maybe we should stop and take a step back. " I hear friends who go on trips to faraway places, look up at the sky, and say, 'Wow, you never see an empty sky anymore,'" McDowell tells me with a touch of sadness and concern. Musk, Bezos, Wisniewski, the Europeans, and the Chinese would argue that we need cheap, ubiquitous internet everywhere in the world, forcivilian and military applications. And of course, there is a lot of money to be made and a genuine need to serve communities in remote locations without having to invest much more money in terrestrial infrastructure, but do we really need to stream TikTok from space?

"I don't necessarily have a position on that," McDowell says. "My position is that even if that's the case, it shouldn't be just the US that decides. It should be decided by all countries around the world because everyone is affected, whether they are space powers or not. And that's the discussion I'm trying to promote: let's have a global conversation, preferably at the UN level, about how to balance the interests of the environment and the space industry more generally."

He's right. And if we all decide that we need this, let's have everyone agree on the best solution to minimize the impact on humanity. The smartest solution. The most technologically advanced.

If we ultimately do this, as a species, let's truly find the smartest and least harmful way, one that doesn't make us all dependent on a man who has shown no consideration for his fellow human beings despite having a savior complex, thinking that only he can guarantee the survival of humanity on a barren red planet.

The fiercest space race is not about returning to the Moon. It's about allowing you to make a TikTok or watch Netflix on your phone anywhere on the planet, from the Atacama salt flats to the Khongor dunes in the Gobi Desert. To make this happen, two radically different design philosophies are at war, and several companies are building the infrastructure necessary to ensure that every phone on the planet is permanently connected to the Internet.

grok: what countries have banned starlink and what are their international freedom scores

No country with a high Freedom House score has imposed a hard ban on Starlink. The places where it is explicitly blocked or blacklisted are almost all rated Not Free, with very low scores on political rights and civil liberties.

Freedom House’s Freedom in the World 2026 (covering 2025) uses a 0–100 scale. Higher is freer. Status is Free / Partly Free / Not Free.⁠Freedomhouse
Explicitly banned or blacklisted

These appear in Starlink’s own availability data and reporting as hard blocks (geofenced, no license, import bans, or official prohibition of terminals):
Country / territoryFreedom House 2026StatusNotes on Starlink
North Korea3Not FreeTotal isolation; no commercial satellite internet of this type.
Belarus7Not FreeNever licensed; regime has said use is not permitted.
Afghanistan8Not FreeBlacklisted; Taliban-era restrictions.
China9Not FreeUnlicensed foreign satellite comms banned; enforcement includes ships in territorial waters. Ban extends to Hong Kong and Macao under PRC telecom rules.
Cuba9Not FreeOften listed as unavailable / restricted.
Iran10Not FreeTerminals formally prohibited; no authorization to operate.
Russia12Not FreeOfficial ban; 2026 decree banned import of foreign satellite terminals on national-security grounds and named Starlink.
Syria~10 (was ~5, +5 in 2025)Not FreeBlacklisted; also tied to sanctions / parent-regime issues.
Hong Kong scores 41 (Partly Free) but is covered by China’s ban.⁠Mappr

These governments treat an independent, foreign-controlled constellation as a threat to information control, data sovereignty, or national security. That tracks with how they treat the open internet generally.
Not the same as a “ban”
Several other countries have denied licenses or sit in regulatory limbo for ownership rules, local-partner requirements, or security reviews—not a blanket geopolitical ban:
Namibia — license refused (51% local ownership rule). Not in the hard-blacklist group.
South Africa — stalled on Black Economic Empowerment ownership rules.
India — license progress but final security clearance delayed at times.
Others in limbo or “coming soon”: parts of North Africa, some Gulf states, etc.

DRC banned then reversed. Papua New Guinea had a legal fight that later eased. Those are regulatory fights, not the same category as Russia or China.

Pattern: Hard bans cluster at the bottom of the Freedom House scale (single digits to low teens). Countries that score in the 80s–100s (Canada, much of Europe, Japan, etc.) have licensed Starlink or are in the process of doing so. The correlation is not accidental: the service is useful precisely where terrestrial networks are weak and where governments want to keep a closed information environment.

text:
Bitchat, the messaging app made by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, has been removed from app stores in India.

Bitchat does not need the internet or a mobile network. Phones close to each other pass messages along over Bluetooth, so it keeps working even during an internet shutdown. Messages are encrypted and there is no central server.

The IT ministry ordered the removal on 3 October under Section 69A of the IT Act, the law the government uses to block websites and apps. The app is gone from Apple's App Store and Google Play in India, and its website does not open on many Indian internet providers.

In July, authorities had already asked GitHub to take down its code. The reason given then was that police cannot easily intercept or trace messages on it, and that it works during shutdowns.

India made up about 85% of all Bitchat downloads in one week of July, up from about 1% the month before.

The Internet Freedom Foundation, a digital rights group, says the law allows blocking unlawful content, not blocking an app because it works during shutdowns.
